title: The Clever Parrot's Lesson
summary: A boastful parrot who always interrupts others to show off what he knows learns, after his wrong advice causes a small mishap, that listening carefully matters more than talking the most.
poll: The person who talks the most in a group usually knows the most.

versions.title: The Parrot Who Listened
versions.text:
A flock of parrots lived in a forest.
They lived in tall trees.
Each day, they flew out to find fruit.
One parrot was named Rami.
Rami talked the most.
He liked to cut off others.
He liked to brag.

One day, the best tree had no fruit.
The flock had to find a new tree.
The flock flew out to look.

A parrot named Tala flew by a river.
She saw some fig trees.
The trees were full of fruit.
She tried to tell the flock.
But Rami cut her off.
He said, "Follow me! I know a way!"

Most of the flock went with Rami.
His way led to a dry place.
It was full of rocks.
There was no fruit there.
The birds grew tired.
They grew hungry too.

They flew back to Kanz.
Kanz was the oldest bird.
Kanz asked Tala to finish.
Tala told them about the fig trees.

This time, all of them listened.
Even Rami listened.
They flew to the fig trees.
They ate well at last.

Rami learned a lesson.
Listening matters more than talking the most.

versions.title: The Clever Parrot's Lesson
versions.text:
In a green forest, a flock of parrots lived together high in the trees.

Every morning, they flew out as a group. They searched for ripe fruit. They searched for hours.

One young parrot named Rami always talked the loudest. He loved to cut off other parrots. He loved to brag about whatever he thought he knew.

One morning, the flock's best tree was bare. They needed to search the forest. They needed to find a new place to eat.

The flock spread out to look. Flying near the river, a quieter parrot named Tala spotted fig trees. The trees were heavy with ripe fruit. She began telling the others about it. But Rami quickly cut her off. "Follow me! I know a faster way!" he announced.

Most of the flock followed Rami. They trusted his loud, confident voice. But his path led only to a dry, rocky area. No fruit grew there. The parrots grew tired and hungry.

Eventually, they flew back to Kanz, the oldest parrot. Kanz asked Tala to finish what she had tried to say. Tala explained about the fig trees near the river.

This time, everyone listened carefully, even Rami. Together, the flock flew to the fig trees. They finally ate well.

Rami learned, at last, that listening carefully matters more than talking the loudest.

versions.title: The Clever Parrot's Lesson
versions.text:
In a lush green forest, a flock of parrots lived together high among the tallest trees.

Every morning, they flew out as a group. They searched the forest for ripe fruit. They searched for most of the day.

One young parrot named Rami always talked the loudest of the flock. He loved to cut off other parrots. He always wanted to brag about whatever he thought he knew best.

One morning, the flock's favorite tree had become bare overnight. They needed to search the wider forest. They needed a new place to find food.

The flock spread out in several directions. Flying near the winding river, a quieter parrot named Tala spotted a row of fig trees. The trees were heavy with ripe fruit. She began telling the others about it. But Rami quickly cut her off before she could finish. "Follow me! I know a faster way to find food!" he announced with great confidence.

Most of the flock followed Rami without question. They trusted his loud, confident voice. But his chosen path led only to a dry, rocky area. No fruit grew there at all. The parrots grew tired and hungry, and increasingly frustrated.

Eventually, the whole flock flew back to Kanz, the oldest parrot in the group. Kanz gently asked Tala to finally finish what she had tried to say. Tala calmly explained about the fig trees near the river.

This time, everyone listened carefully from start to finish, even Rami himself. Together, the flock flew straight to the fig trees. They finally ate well.

Rami learned, at last, that listening carefully matters more than talking the loudest.

versions.title: The Clever Parrot's Lesson
versions.text:
In a lush, green forest, a flock of parrots lived together high among the tallest trees. They spent their days in search of food. Every morning, the whole flock flew out together to search the forest for ripe fruit.

One young parrot named Rami was famously boastful. He always talked the loudest of the flock. He loved to interrupt other parrots. He was always eager to brag about whatever he thought he already knew.

One morning, the flock found that their best fruit tree had become bare overnight. They needed to search the wider forest for a new place to find food.

The flock spread out in several directions to search. Flying near the winding river, a quieter parrot named Tala spotted a row of fig trees heavy with ripe fruit. She began telling the others about her find. But Rami quickly interrupted her before she could finish. "Follow me! I know a much faster way to find food!" he said with great confidence.

Most of the flock followed Rami without question. They trusted his loud voice over Tala's quieter one. But his chosen path turned out to be a mistake. It led only to a dry, rocky area where no fruit grew at all. The parrots grew tired and hungry, and more and more upset.

Eventually, the whole flock flew back to Kanz, the oldest and wisest parrot in the group. Kanz asked Tala to finally finish what she had tried to say before Rami's interruption. Tala calmly explained about the fig trees she had spotted near the river.

This time, everyone listened carefully from start to finish, even Rami, without a single interruption. Together, the flock flew straight to the fig trees and finally ate well.

Rami finally saw his mistake. He learned that listening carefully matters far more than talking the loudest or interrupting the most.

versions.title: The Clever Parrot's Lesson: Listening Over Boasting
versions.text:
In a lush, green forest, a flock of parrots lived together high among the tallest trees, spending their days moving from branch to branch in a constant search for food and shelter from the midday heat. Every morning, the whole flock flew out together to search the wider forest for ripe, juicy fruit before the rising temperatures made flying difficult.

One young parrot named Rami was famously boastful and overconfident, consistently talking the loudest of the entire flock regardless of the situation or who else happened to be speaking. He loved interrupting other parrots mid-sentence, always eager to brag about whatever he assumed he already understood better than anyone else, without ever pausing to consider the consequences of acting on incomplete information.

One morning, the flock discovered, to their dismay, that their favorite fruit tree had become completely bare overnight, its branches picked clean by other hungry creatures passing through. They now needed to search the wider forest carefully for a brand-new source of food before everyone grew too hungry and exhausted to fly much farther.

The flock spread out in several directions to search. Flying near the winding river, a quieter, more attentive parrot named Tala spotted a row of fig trees heavy with perfectly ripe fruit. She began telling the others excitedly about her discovery, but Rami, true to form, interrupted her before she could finish a single sentence. "Follow me! I know a much faster way to find plenty of food!" he announced with entirely unearned confidence. The other parrots, accustomed to following whoever spoke loudest and first, trusted Rami's overconfident voice over Tala's quieter, more careful one, never pausing to ask whether he actually knew where he was leading them.

His misguided confidence led the flock only to a dry, rocky area where no fruit grew at all, a direct consequence of acting on an interrupted, incomplete idea rather than full information. The parrots grew tired, hungry, and increasingly frustrated with every wasted minute.

Eventually, the flock flew back to Kanz, the oldest and wisest parrot in the group. Kanz gently asked Tala to finally finish what she had tried to say before Rami's interruption. Tala calmly explained the fig trees she had spotted near the river, information that could have spared the entire flock a wasted, hungry morning.

This time, every parrot listened attentively from start to finish, even Rami himself, without a single interruption. Together, they flew straight to the fig trees and finally ate well.

Rami finally recognized the consequence of his overconfidence and gained real wisdom: listening attentively matters far more than talking the loudest or interrupting the most.

versions.title: The Clever Parrot's Lesson: Listening Over Boasting
versions.text:
High among the tallest trees of a lush, green forest, a flock of parrots lived together, spending their days moving continuously from branch to branch in search of food and shelter from the midday heat that settled heavily over the canopy each afternoon; every morning, the entire flock flew out collectively to search the wider forest for ripe fruit before rising temperatures made comfortable flying increasingly difficult.

Among them was a young parrot named Rami, famously boastful and overconfident, who consistently talked louder than every other member of the flock regardless of circumstance, taking particular pleasure in interrupting others mid-sentence and boasting about whatever he presumed he already understood more thoroughly than anyone else, all without ever pausing to consider the potential consequences of acting upon incomplete information gathered hastily rather than through patient, methodical observation.

One particular morning, the flock discovered, to their considerable dismay, that their customary fruit tree had become entirely bare overnight, its branches stripped clean by other hungry creatures, compelling them to search the wider forest meticulously for an alternative source of food before exhaustion prevented further flight. As the flock dispersed in search of options, a quieter, considerably more attentive parrot named Tala, flying near the winding river, spotted a row of fig trees laden with perfectly ripened fruit—precisely the discovery the flock urgently required—and began informing the others with evident excitement, only for Rami, entirely true to form, to interrupt her before she could complete even a single sentence: "Follow me! I know a considerably faster way to locate abundant food!" he proclaimed with thoroughly unearned confidence, and the remaining parrots, long habituated to following whichever voice spoke loudest and first, trusted his overconfident declaration over Tala's quieter, more measured one without ever pausing to question whether he genuinely understood their destination.

His fundamentally misguided confidence ultimately led the flock only toward a dry, rocky expanse devoid of any fruit whatsoever, a direct and predictable consequence of acting upon an interrupted, incomplete notion rather than comprehensive, carefully gathered information, and the parrots grew progressively tired, hungry, and increasingly frustrated with each successive, wasted minute.

Eventually, the flock returned to Kanz, the eldest and unquestionably wisest parrot within the group, who gently requested that Tala finally complete what she had originally attempted to communicate before Rami's interruption; Tala calmly explained the location of the fig trees she had spotted near the river, information that could have spared the entire flock an unnecessarily wasted, hungry morning had anyone paused to listen from the outset.

On this occasion, every parrot listened with complete attentiveness from beginning to end, including Rami himself, without a single further interruption, and together they flew directly toward the fig trees, ultimately consuming as much ripened fruit as they desired.

From that transformative morning onward, Rami genuinely recognized the consequence of his habitual overconfidence and acquired authentic wisdom: listening attentively, he came to realize, matters considerably more than talking the loudest or interrupting most frequently.

keyWords.definition: a colorful bird that can copy sounds and words it hears
keyWords.example: The parrot on my uncle's farm can say "good morning" every day.

keyWords.definition: a group of birds or other animals that stay and travel together
keyWords.example: A flock of pigeons landed together in the busy park.

keyWords.definition: to pay attention to sounds or to what someone is saying
keyWords.example: Please listen carefully to the directions before you start.

keyWords.definition: the sweet, juicy part of a plant that people and animals eat
keyWords.example: We picked ripe fruit from the trees in our garden.

keyWords.definition: a large area of land covered with many trees
keyWords.example: The hikers walked quietly through the shady forest.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A parrot who learns that listening matters more than talking the most
A flock of birds that moves to a new forest every single year to find warm weather
A river full of fish that the parrots like to eat for dinner every evening
A young parrot who teaches the whole flock how to fly south before the winter
questions.why: The story follows Rami as his interrupting causes a mistake, and he learns that listening carefully matters more than talking the most.

wrong.B: The flock does not move to a new forest every year in the story.
wrong.C: The story is about fruit, not fish.
wrong.D: Rami does not teach the flock how to fly.

questions.stem: Why did the flock need to search for a new place to find food?
options: The river had completely dried up during the night
A sudden storm had destroyed most of the forest's trees
Their favorite fruit tree had become completely bare
The flock simply wanted to explore a brand-new forest
questions.why: The story says the flock's favorite fruit tree had become completely bare, so they needed to search for food elsewhere.

wrong.A: The story does not mention the river drying up.
wrong.B: No storm is described in the story.
wrong.D: The flock searches out of need, not simply to explore.

questions.stem: What did Tala discover near the river?
options: A dry, rocky place with no fruit anywhere nearby
A group of birds from a faraway forest
A nest that another flock had left behind
A row of fig trees full of ripe, juicy fruit
questions.why: Tala spotted a row of fig trees heavy with ripe fruit near the river, which she tried to tell the flock about.

wrong.A: The dry, rocky place is where Rami's path led, not what Tala found.
wrong.B: No other flock of birds is found near the river.
wrong.C: No abandoned nest is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: Why did most of the flock follow Rami instead of listening to Tala?
options: They trusted Rami's loud, confident voice instead
Tala had already flown far away from the group
Kanz told them to follow Rami's direction instead
Rami promised to share extra fruit with everyone
questions.why: The flock was used to trusting whoever spoke loudest and first, so they followed Rami's confident voice instead of Tala.

wrong.B: Tala was right there with the flock, not far away.
wrong.C: Kanz does not appear until after the flock returns.
wrong.D: Rami does not promise anyone extra fruit.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Rami's chosen path from what the flock found there?
options: It led to a lake full of fresh, clean water
It was a careless guess that turned out to be wrong
It was actually shorter than Tala's suggested path
It led straight to the fig trees by the river
questions.why: Since Rami's path led only to a dry, rocky area with no fruit, it shows his confident claim was really just a careless, wrong guess.

wrong.A: No lake is found along Rami's path.
wrong.C: The story never compares the length of the two paths.
wrong.D: Rami's path led away from the fig trees, not toward them.

questions.stem: Why did Kanz ask Tala to finish what she had tried to say earlier?
options: Kanz did not trust anything that Rami had said that day
Kanz wanted Tala to apologize to the whole flock
Kanz wanted to hear the information Rami had interrupted
Kanz had forgotten where the old fruit tree was
questions.why: Kanz realized Tala had important information that was cut off, so Kanz asked her to finally share it.

wrong.A: Kanz does not simply distrust Rami; Kanz wants more information.
wrong.B: Tala did nothing wrong, so there is no reason to apologize.
wrong.D: The old fruit tree's location is not the issue here.

questions.stem: In the story, what does it mean that the flock 'listened carefully' the second time?
options: They quickly flew away before anyone finished speaking
They argued loudly about which path to follow
They ignored every single word that was being said
They paid close, full attention without interrupting
questions.why: Listening carefully means paying close, full attention, which is exactly what the flock did for Tala the second time.

wrong.A: Flying away would mean not listening at all.
wrong.B: The flock does not argue the second time.
wrong.C: Ignoring would mean the opposite of listening carefully.

questions.stem: Why does the story end by saying Rami learned that listening matters more than talking?
options: To show that parrots cannot ever learn new things from others
To teach that paying attention is more valuable than boasting
To explain exactly how fig trees grow fruit each year in the oasis
To show that Kanz was the fastest flyer in the flock of parrots
questions.why: The ending shows Rami's change and teaches readers that paying careful attention is more valuable than talking or boasting the most.

wrong.A: Rami's change shows that he can learn, not that he cannot.
wrong.C: The story does not explain how fig trees grow fruit.
wrong.D: The story never compares flying speed between the parrots.

LOW.prompt: Why did Rami's plan lead the flock to a place with no fruit? Explain using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I explained why Rami's plan failed.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: Rami's plan failed because he interrupted Tala before she could finish telling the flock about the fig trees she had found. He said he knew a faster way, but he was only guessing, and his way led to a dry, rocky place with no fruit at all. The flock followed him anyway because they trusted his loud, confident voice instead of waiting to hear what Tala actually knew.

keyWords.definition: to start talking or doing something before another person has finished
keyWords.example: It is polite to wait your turn instead of interrupting someone who is speaking.

keyWords.definition: often bragging about yourself in a way that annoys other people
keyWords.example: The boastful runner kept telling everyone he would win the race easily.

keyWords.definition: something done wrong, often by accident or without enough thought
keyWords.example: Forgetting to check the map was a costly mistake on our hiking trip.
We had to search the whole house before we finally found the missing keys.

keyWords.definition: paying close attention in order to avoid mistakes or danger
keyWords.example: The careful driver checked both mirrors before changing lanes.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: A boastful parrot learns that careful listening beats loud talking
A flock of parrots decides to leave their forest forever
A quiet parrot becomes the fastest flyer in the whole group
A river suddenly dries up and the whole forest disappears
questions.why: The story shows how Rami's boastful interrupting caused a mistake, and how he eventually learns that careful listening matters more than loud talking.

wrong.B: The flock searches for food, but it does not leave the forest forever.
wrong.C: Tala is careful and observant, but the story is not about flying speed.
wrong.D: The river is not described as drying up or the forest disappearing.

questions.stem: What was Rami's most noticeable habit within the flock?
options: He always searched for food alone, far from the group
He constantly interrupted others and bragged about himself
He carefully listened to every single parrot who spoke
He never spoke at all during the flock's daily search
questions.why: The story describes Rami as famously boastful, constantly interrupting others and bragging about what he thought he knew.

wrong.A: Rami searches together with the flock, not alone.
wrong.C: Careful listening is Tala's habit, not Rami's, at first.
wrong.D: Rami talks the loudest of the entire flock; he does not stay silent.

questions.stem: Why did Rami's chosen path turn out to be a mistake?
options: He had carefully studied the entire forest beforehand
Kanz had secretly told him to lead the flock there
He interrupted Tala before she could share full information
He was searching for a river instead of fruit trees
questions.why: Because Rami cut Tala off before she finished, he led the flock based on an incomplete idea, which turned out to be a mistake.

wrong.A: Rami's path was a guess, not based on careful study.
wrong.B: Kanz does not appear until after the flock's mistake.
wrong.D: Rami was searching for fruit, not specifically for a river.

questions.stem: What does the flock's choice to follow Rami suggest about the group?
options: They always searched for food in complete silence
They valued a loud, confident voice over careful information
They never trusted any parrot's directions at all
They had already visited the fig trees many times before
questions.why: Because the flock followed Rami's confident shouting rather than waiting for Tala's full, careful explanation, they clearly valued loudness over careful information.

wrong.A: Both Rami and the narrator describe plenty of talking, not silence.
wrong.C: The flock did trust Rami's directions, just the wrong parrot's.
wrong.D: The fig trees were a new discovery that morning.

questions.stem: What did the flock find when they reached the place Rami led them to?
options: A dry, rocky area with no fruit growing at all
A row of fig trees heavy with ripe fruit
A careful map showing the whole forest's rivers
A group of other parrots searching nearby
questions.why: Rami's chosen path led only to a dry, rocky area where no fruit grew at all.

wrong.B: The fig trees were where Tala had spotted fruit, not Rami's path.
wrong.C: No map is mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: No other group of parrots is found there.

questions.stem: Why did Kanz specifically ask Tala to finish her earlier thought?
options: Kanz wanted to find out why the search had gone wrong
Kanz had completely forgotten about the missing fruit tree
Kanz wanted Tala to admit she had made a mistake
Kanz needed help searching for a place to rest
questions.why: After the wasted morning, Kanz wanted to understand what had gone wrong, so Kanz asked Tala to finish the explanation Rami had interrupted.

wrong.B: The missing fruit tree is the reason the search began, not something Kanz forgot.
wrong.C: Tala made no mistake; Rami's interruption caused the problem.
wrong.D: The flock is not searching for a place to rest.

questions.stem: In the story, what does it mean that Tala was 'careful' in her search?
options: She searched quickly without paying much attention
She interrupted other parrots while they were speaking
She paid close attention and noticed small details
She bragged loudly about what she had already found
questions.why: Being careful means paying close attention, which is how Tala managed to notice the fig trees that others missed.

wrong.A: Careful searching is thorough, not quick and inattentive.
wrong.B: Tala is the one interrupted, not the one interrupting.
wrong.D: Tala calmly explains her discovery; she does not boast.

questions.stem: How does the story organize Rami's mistake and the flock's final success?
options: It lists the exact steps for building a parrot's nest
It compares two different forests from long ago
It describes one calm day with absolutely no searching
It shows a boastful mistake, then a careful, listening success
questions.why: The story first shows how Rami's boastful interruption leads to a mistake, then shows how careful listening finally leads to success.

wrong.A: The story does not describe building a nest.
wrong.B: No other forest or earlier time period is compared.
wrong.C: The whole story centers on the flock's search for food.

MID.prompt: Explain how Rami changed from the beginning of the story to the end. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: At the beginning of the story, Rami was boastful and always interrupted other parrots, including Tala, just to brag about what he thought he knew. This habit caused a mistake, since his guess about a faster path led the whole flock to a dry, rocky area with no fruit. By the end, Rami recognized his mistake and listened carefully, without interrupting, while Tala finally explained about the fig trees by the river, which let the whole flock eat well.

keyWords.definition: too sure of yourself or your own ideas, more than the facts actually support
keyWords.example: The overconfident chess player ignored a clear trap and lost the game quickly.

keyWords.definition: paying close, focused attention to someone or something
keyWords.example: The attentive student noticed a small detail that everyone else had missed.

keyWords.definition: based on a wrong idea or poor judgment, even if well-intended
keyWords.example: His misguided plan to shortcut through the swamp only cost the hikers more time.

keyWords.definition: good judgment gained through experience and careful thought
keyWords.example: The elder's wisdom helped the young farmers avoid a costly mistake.

keyWords.definition: a result or effect that happens because of an earlier action
keyWords.example: Skipping practice had a clear consequence: the team lost the next match.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: Overconfidence and constant interrupting lead to mistakes that attentive listening prevents
Forests always recover quickly whenever a tree runs out of fruit, so parrots never worry
Older parrots always make far better decisions than younger ones, so the young must obey
Rivers are the only genuinely reliable food source in any forest, so parrots stay by the water
questions.why: The story shows how Rami's overconfident interrupting caused a wasted search, while attentive listening later led the flock to success.

wrong.B: The story does not claim forests always recover quickly.
wrong.C: The story is about listening versus boasting, not simply age.
wrong.D: Fig trees near the river, not the river itself, provide the food.

questions.stem: Why did the flock end up in a dry, rocky area with no fruit?
options: Tala had deliberately misled them away from the fig trees
They acted on Rami's misguided, overconfident interruption
Kanz had ordered the flock to search in that direction
A sudden storm forced the flock to land there instead
questions.why: The flock followed Rami's confident but misguided claim, made by interrupting Tala before she finished, which led them to the fruitless area.

wrong.A: Tala never tries to mislead the flock; she tries to help them.
wrong.C: Kanz appears only after the flock returns, not before.
wrong.D: No storm is mentioned as a reason for the detour.

questions.stem: What does Tala's behavior suggest about the value of attentive observation?
options: Attentive observation is slower and therefore less useful
Attentive observation only matters near rivers and forests
Attentive observation often reveals what loud confidence misses
Attentive observation always requires help from older parrots
questions.why: Tala's quiet, attentive search found the fig trees that Rami's loud, overconfident guessing completely missed.

wrong.A: Tala's attentive search is what actually finds the food, showing its value.
wrong.B: The lesson about attention applies generally, not only near rivers.
wrong.D: Tala makes her discovery on her own, before Kanz is even involved.

questions.stem: In the story, what does it mean that Rami's confidence was 'misguided'?
options: His confidence was based on careful, attentive research
His confidence convinced the whole flock to trust him forever
His confidence helped the flock find fruit more quickly
His confidence was based on a mistaken, incomplete idea
questions.why: Misguided means based on a wrong idea, which fits Rami's confident claim that was really just a guess made after interrupting Tala.

wrong.A: Rami's confidence was not based on careful research; it was a guess.
wrong.B: The flock's trust in Rami is shaken after the mistake, not strengthened forever.
wrong.C: His confidence led the flock away from food, not toward it.

questions.stem: What consequence did the flock face as a direct result of Rami's interruption?
options: They wasted a hungry morning searching a fruitless area
They discovered an entirely new river to drink from
They decided to permanently exclude Rami from the flock
They found twice as much fruit as they had expected
questions.why: Because Rami interrupted Tala and led the flock on a guess, the direct consequence was a wasted, hungry morning in an area with no fruit.

wrong.B: No new river is discovered in the story.
wrong.C: Rami remains part of the flock throughout the story.
wrong.D: The flock found no fruit at all on Rami's path, not extra fruit.

questions.stem: Put these events in the correct order.
options: The flock finds no fruit, Rami interrupts, Tala spots the fig trees
Tala spots the fig trees, Rami interrupts, the flock finds no fruit
Rami interrupts, the flock finds no fruit, Tala spots the fig trees
The flock finds no fruit, Tala spots the fig trees, Rami interrupts
questions.why: Tala first spots the fig trees, then Rami interrupts her before she can finish, and only afterward does the flock find no fruit on his path.

wrong.A: The flock cannot find no fruit before Rami even interrupts Tala.
wrong.C: Rami's interruption must come after Tala's discovery, not before it.
wrong.D: Rami's interruption happens right after Tala's discovery, before the flock finds no fruit.

questions.stem: What allowed the flock to finally succeed in finding food?
options: Rami's continued overconfidence in his own instincts
A second, luckier guess about which direction to fly
The whole flock's attentive patience in letting Tala finish
Kanz personally leading the flock to the fig trees
questions.why: The flock finally succeeded because everyone, including Rami, listened attentively and let Tala finish explaining where the fig trees were.

wrong.A: Rami's overconfidence is what caused the earlier mistake.
wrong.B: The second attempt relies on Tala's real information, not another guess.
wrong.D: Kanz asks Tala to explain; Kanz does not personally lead the flight.

questions.stem: Why does the author have Rami, rather than Tala, undergo the clearest change by the story's end?
options: To prove that older parrots never need to change their habits, no matter what happens to them
To show that Tala was never truly capable of leading the flock over the mountains
To explain in detail how parrots build their nests near the rivers in the hot season
To highlight the wisdom gained when overconfidence gives way to attentive listening
questions.why: By showing Rami move from boastful interrupting to attentive listening, the author highlights the wisdom gained when overconfidence gives way to careful attention.

wrong.A: Kanz, who is older, is not the one changing in the story.
wrong.B: Tala proves capable; it is her careful discovery that saves the flock.
wrong.C: The story never describes how parrots build nests.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says the person who talks the most in a group usually knows the most. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Rami and Tala.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that the person who talks the most in a group usually knows the most. In the story, Rami talked the loudest and interrupted Tala, yet his overconfident, misguided guess led the whole flock to a dry, rocky area with no fruit. Tala, who spoke the least at first, actually held the valuable information, since she had carefully spotted the fig trees by the river. Someone might argue that a confident voice is reassuring in the moment, but the consequence in the story shows that attentive listening, not loud talking, is what actually finds the food.
